speaker: patient
text: That's a really hard question. I feel like I'm the one who always hears a promise where there isn't one. To prevent someone else from doing that... I guess I'd have to be really careful with my words. I'd probably say something like, "This is just a thought, and it might not work at all, but maybe we could..." or "Don't count on this yet, but what if..." I would be so scared of getting their hopes up and then disappointing them. It feels like I'm setting a trap for myself, where I'll end up feeling guilty no matter what. It seems safer to just not suggest things at all.

text: That's... really hard. My first instinct is to just agree to whatever it is to avoid being difficult. But if I had to ask for time... I guess I'd try to make it sound like it's my own issue. I might say something like, "That sounds interesting, thank you. Can I have a little time to think about it? I just need to process things a bit so I can give you a proper answer." Even saying that feels like I'm being a bother, like I'm making them wait. I'd be worried they'd hear it as me not being interested. It’s hard to ask for time without feeling like I’m being rude.

speaker: patient
text: A useful repair... that's hard. My instinct is to just erase my own needs completely. But if I were trying to do better, I guess it would involve acknowledging their excitement but not completely abandoning my own point. I could say something like, "Oh, I get it, thanks for telling me. I'm not mad at all." Then, instead of just dropping it, maybe I could add, "I just lose my train of thought really easily, so it helps me if we can go one at a time." That way, I'm still reassuring them, which I need to do to feel safe, but I'm not taking back my request. It feels a little more... solid? Like my need didn't just vanish because they weren't being malicious.
